A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PAPAGEI and provide readable methods, equations, results, figures, and complete appendices. Retained content can be matched across reorganization and renumbering. Internal inconsistencies in some new v2 results limit their interpretation but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and regression experiments across 20 tasks, together with component, scaling, data-efficiency, and skin-tone analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds demographic prediction, demographic and morphology-feature controls, and statistical analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix E introduces an evaluated PAPAGEI-S variant combining learned embeddings with age and sex, changing downstream predictor inputs. The core encoder, participant and morphology pairing strategies, and expert heads remain. Revisions to the contrastive-loss equations do not establish that the retained models' implementations changed.

E1.justification: The original training datasets and 20-task benchmark remain. v2 adds age regression, age classification, and sex classification on VitalDB, MESA, and MIMIC-III in Table 16, extending task coverage without introducing new datasets.

E2.justification: Table 15 adds evaluated demographics-only, morphology-only, and combined demographics-plus-morphology baselines, alongside PAPAGEI-S plus demographics. These substantially expand controls for what learned representations contribute. The original REGLE, Chronos, MOMENT, SimCLR, BYOL, TF-C, and statistical-feature comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 and Tables 3–4 add sMAPE for aggregating regression performance, supplementing MAE. Appendix E specifies ridge and logistic regression for the new feature controls. Existing subject-level splits and stated training budgets remain; newly disclosed model-selection and windowing details do not establish changes to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of whether demographics and handcrafted morphology features explain PAPAGEI's performance, and whether demographics complement its embeddings (Appendix E). Appendix D.5 tests the relationship between SQI and unavailable IPA. Expanded prediction analyses include gestational-age bimodality and additional blood-pressure cases. Existing component, scaling, and pre-training-data ablations are retained and refined.

E5.justification: Beyond the existing 500-resample confidence intervals, v2 adds Wilcoxon tests to ablations, Friedman testing and critical-difference diagrams, 1,000 confidence-interval score-sampling repetitions repeated five times, and a 1,000-permutation IPA/SQI test. Figure 9 gains error bars. Appendix A first discloses five pre-training iterations, without establishing an increase over v1 or reporting seeds.

E6.justification: The principal benchmark scores remain, but v2 adds demographic results, per-task component results, sMAPE values, and statistical findings. Existing ablation values also change: VitalDB-only pre-training MAE changes from 11.45 in v1 Figure 6 to 12.29 in v2 Figure 5. New demographic reporting is inconsistent: Table 16 gives age MAE 8.78 and sex AUROC 0.74, while the prose gives 7.78 and 0.79.

T1.justification: The contrastive-loss mathematics is revised beyond notation. In the morphology loss, the denominator changes from excluding the positive index j to excluding the anchor i, and bidirectional batch averaging is explicitly reformulated. These are limited mathematical corrections; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The open-model, training-scale, benchmark-coverage, and efficiency claims retain their scope. The conclusion newly asserts robustness to class imbalance and broad R2 superiority using results already present in v1. Its seven-task R2 superiority claim for PAPAGEI-S overstates Tables 11–12, which include wins by PAPAGEI-P and other methods.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of demographic confounding and complementary information, and explains demographic-prediction differences through patient pairing and device heterogeneity. It identifies failure to capture gestational-age bimodality, discusses unavailable demographic inputs, and narrows scaling conclusions to the present training data. Appendix I adds concrete distribution-shift and adaptation directions, presented as future work.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly details matched baseline settings, tested temperatures, task-specific selection among pretrained models, and training-versus-inference parameter accounting. Appendix B adds PPG-DaLiA's eight-second windows, six-second overlap, and two-second shift. The reproducibility statement changes from promised release to reported publication of resources. These are substantial disclosures, not evidence of smaller architectures or rerun experiments.

R1.justification: The open, PPG-specific positioning remains. v2 sharpens comparisons with Abbaspourazad et al., adds Table 17 comparing prior PPG studies' data, devices, openness, and tasks, and extends discussion with references such as Lai et al. and Narayanswamy et al. This develops the existing positioning rather than replacing it.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and several results discussions receive substantial rewriting. Contributions become separate paragraphs, ablations are reordered, Section 6 becomes Discussion & Conclusion, and the appendices gain a reorganized analytical structure. These changes extend beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with clearer embedding labels; ablation plots gain significance annotations and revised axes. Regression plots are redesigned, with the retained heart-rate case moved into expanded Figure 25. v2 adds Tables 14–17 and statistical Figures 22–24, changes table headers to inference parameter counts, and adds skin-tone error bars.

improvement.justification: Table 15 supplies useful demographic and handcrafted-feature controls absent from v1, Appendix D.5 tests the SQI rationale, and Appendix A makes model selection and inference costs more transparent. These improve interpretability and reproducibility while retaining the original benchmark evidence. The gains are limited by conflicting demographic results, overstated concluding claims, and insufficient explanation of the confidence-interval score-sampling procedure used to support stronger significance claims.
